name: Executive order of September 13, 1882 restoring the greater part of the Malheur Reservation to the public domain
nations: Wadatika and other Snake or Paiute bands of the Malheur country (Northern Paiute), today the Burns Paiute Tribe
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It restored to the public domain all of the Malheur Reservation south of the fourth standard parallel south, except 320 acres (the north half of the old Camp Harney military post), and all of it north of that parallel and west of the range line between ranges 33 and 34 East (Royce p. 908).
Royce's note says this order relinquished the tract in solid mauve, including the south half of Camp Harney, and that the order of May 21, 1883 took the rest except 320 acres (Royce pp. 911 and 913).

breaches.what: The Commission found the bands were deprived of their title to the Malheur Reservation land in January 1879, when the United States forcibly removed them to the Yakima Reservation and restored the land to the public domain without their consent or payment. Finding 36 records that on September 13, 1882 the President restored the greater portion of the reservation to the public domain after Oregon appeals, and finding 37 that none of the land was sold for the bands' benefit and they were never compensated.

landTaken: The greater portion of the Malheur Reservation (Commission finding 36). No acreage figure for this order was found in a source opened.
compensation: The Commission valued the land at $579,722.00 as of January 1879, less offsets (Second Interlocutory Order, April 15, 1959). Interior described the judgment as $567,000 and said fees and expenses reduced it to $468,395.50, which with interest stood at $519,827.49 on June 5, 1963 (press release, 1963).
today: The Burns Paiute Tribe lives near Burns, Oregon, on the edge of the former reservation (Commission finding 38). This is the same January 1879 taking already recorded under cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake and the other Malheur entries; it is counted once.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its ancestors refused to cede any of their lands, that the Malheur executive order reservation of 1.8 million acres was short-lived, and that after the Bannock War the survivors were marched over 300 miles in deep snow to Fort Simcoe and Fort Vancouver.

treaties.json error: presentDayTribes is empty for this record; the Burns Paiute Tribe should be listed. It also links a statute file (638c.pdf) for what Royce lists as an executive order. Not edited.
The Burns Paiute page dates the reservation to 1869; Royce and the Commission give September 12, 1872 for the first order.

Audit 2026-11-08: the Royce source for the Malheur note was cited as p. 910; the note is on p. 911 (p. 910 has the May 21, 1883 order). Corrected. Docket 17 findings 36, 37 and 41, the quote, the $579,722.00 value and the 1963 Interior release were re-read and match.

Camp Harney decision (audit 2026-11-08): Docket 17 covers the 320 acres. Finding 3 defines the land as the January 28, 1876 reservation by metes and bounds, with no exception for Camp Harney; Royce p. 903 says the 640-acre Camp Harney reserve "was already within the general outboundaries of the Malheur reservation"; finding 40 holds aboriginal title to all land within those boundaries and finding 41 that it was taken in January 1879; finding 37 names the March 2, 1889 restoration of the 320 acres and says the bands were never compensated for any reservation land. So the 1889 loss of the 320 acres is part of the same Docket 17 taking. Left uncertain: whether the 640 acres were counted in the stipulated 1,449,305.77 net acres valued (the stipulation lists no military-reserve deduction, Opinion of April 15, 1959). cession-1889-03-02-malheur-indian-reservation-shoshone-snak should be broken with sameEventAs cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. Presidential orders from 1872 set apart the Malheur Reservation in Oregon for the Paiute bands; this 1882 order returned most of it to the public domain.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found the bands were forcibly removed in 1879 and the land restored without consent or payment. Interior admitted in 1963 the 1882 and 1883 orders paid nothing.
plain.today: The Commission valued the land at $579,722.00; Interior described a $567,000 judgment. This is the same taking shown on the other Malheur entries.
